subject: Dedicated capacity commitment — Orbitron: KV offload & quantization tradeoffs
messages:
From: Alex Perez <alex.perez@orbitron.ai>
To: olga_petrov <olga.petrov@redwood.ai>
Cc: sofia.ruiz <sofia.ruiz@orbitron.ai>
Date: Wed, 18 Nov 2026 09:14:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity inquiry — Orbitron expected profile and constraints

Hi Olga,

Thanks again for taking the call earlier. Quick recap from our side and a request for a conservative capacity estimate we can use internally for budget planning:

- Workload: multi-turn Retrieval-Augmented Generation across customer support flows. Typical conversation: 700–2,500 tokens; occasional long sessions up to ~40k tokens (rare, 1–2% of calls).
- QPS: steady-state 35 reqs/s, daily peak 110 reqs/s for short sessions; long-session mix lowers effective throughput due to KV growth.
- Model: we'd like to run the open Llama-derived 70B variant you recommend.
- Requirement: committed reserved pool with SLA for 99th percentile latency at or below 350 ms for short sessions.
- Preference: minimize incremental cost vs on-demand; open to quantized variants if quality impact < 2% on BLEU-like metric.

Can you provide a short plan: suggested GPU reserve count (by GPU type), expected memory headroom assumptions, recommended quantization mode(s) and an approach for handling the 40k sessions without breaking the latency SLA?

Attachments: we included an example tail-session export and our hourly QPS curve.

Appreciate a compact recommendation we can present to finance early next week.

—Alex

From: olga_petrov <olga.petrov@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Perez <alex.perez@orbitron.ai>
Cc: marcus_lin <marcus.lin@redwood.ai>, dev_patel <dev.patel@redwood.ai>
Date: Thu, 19 Nov 2026 14:06:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity inquiry — Orbitron expected profile and constraints

Alex —

Thanks for the clear profile. I ran a quick back-of-envelope and attached a workbook with per-model memory math and trade-offs. Key takeaways up-front:

1) Baseline footprint (fp16): the 70B variant at 64k context (to be conservative for your 40k tail) needs ~72–80 GB GPU memory just for model params + KV headroom at typical per-token KV sizing. That pushes us to 80GB-class GPUs (A800/ H100 80GB equivalent) and a reserve of 6–8 GPUs to meet steady QPS while preserving headroom for spikes.

2) Quantization impact: switching to aggressive int8 (post-training dynamic quant) reduces the model param footprint by ~40–50% in practice for Llama-derived weights, which trades memory for slightly increased decode time. With int8 we estimate the per-GPU headroom requirement drops so a pool of 5 reserved A800-80 GPUs can hit your steady-state and weekday peaks; 99th percentile for short sessions remains within 300–360 ms depending on batching. NF4-like quant (4-bit groupwise) gives the most memory saving (~55–60%) but is higher risk for quality regressions on your RAG prompts.

3) Long-session strategy (40k sessions): we advise a hybrid KV-offload policy — keep KV cache in GPU until session length ~8k tokens, then stream older KV entries to a hot-host-resident cache (NVMe-backed) with RDMA read-ahead. This keeps tail latency for short sessions low while allowing very long sessions to continue with a latency penalty only on the long-request start/refresh operations. In our sim (attached kv-offload-sim-20261118.csv) this approach keeps 99th short-session latency < 400 ms and keeps average cpu I/O overhead modest.

4) Recommended reserved commitment (conservative plan for contract):
   - Plan A (balanced risk): 5x A800-80GB reserved GPUs, default to int8 quant with per-route quality checks and automatic fallback to fp16 for flagged prompts. Include 2x on-demand warm GPUs for burst handling.
   - Plan B (low-risk, higher-cost): 8x A800-80GB reserved GPUs in fp16, with aggressive KV offload threshold at 12k tokens to reduce headroom pressure.

5) Rollout and validation: staged rollout using canary routes. Start with int8 for low-risk tenants and hold ~10% traffic on fp16 to compare quality metrics. We’ll wire eval hooks to your BLEU-like metric so we can auto-detect regressions >2%.

Next steps I recommend: Marcus and I will finalize the capacity workbook (attached) with the exact per-token math and sample throughput curves; Dev will draft a SOW with the two pricing options above and the automatic-fallback policy. Can you confirm which Plan (A or B) you want us to price into the SOW? Also, do you need SOC2 evidence before we sign a commit?

—Olga

From: Alex Perez <alex.perez@orbitron.ai>
To: olga_petrov <olga.petrov@redwood.ai>
Cc: sofia.ruiz <sofia.ruiz@orbitron.ai>
Date: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 10:22:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity commitment — Orbitron: KV offload & quantization tradeoffs

Olga / Marcus —

Thanks, this is exactly the level we needed. Two quick questions before we pick Plan A vs B for finance:

1) When you say fallback to fp16 for flagged prompts — how seamless is that from a per-request routing perspective? Is there a risk of cold-start latency if we flip routes?
2) For the long-session offload path — what tail penalty should we plan for the first offload read (i.e., when older KV pages are fetched back)? Your sim hints at a 120–200 ms penalty per read; can you confirm the expectation and whether that stacks for multi-page reads?

If answers look acceptable we’ll push Plan A to finance and ask for the draft SOW. Also yes — SOC2 Type II evidence is required before a legal commit.

—Alex

From: olga_petrov <olga.petrov@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Perez <alex.perez@orbitron.ai>
Cc: marcus_lin <marcus.lin@redwood.ai>, dev_patel <dev.patel@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 22 Nov 2026 16:42:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity commitment — Orbitron: KV offload & quantization tradeoffs

Alex — quick answers and actions:

1) Seamless per-request fallback: our routing layer supports per-request model variant selection. We implement a per-route header that tags requests for int8 or fp16; the switch path is a fast route mux without cold-start as long as both model variants are resident in the cluster (we will keep a small fp16 standby for that reason). If both variants are not resident (cost tradeoff), the platform will warm on-demand — that can add 150–350 ms depending on model and sequence length. For Plan A we explicitly keep the standby fp16 replica so fallback latency is <40 ms for short sessions.

2) Offload read penalty: sim shows a single-page (8–16k token chunk) read ~120–220 ms depending on NIC/NDMA and whether prefetch is in place. Multi-page reads do stack, but our offload policy uses progressive prefetch (read-ahead) so the observable user-facing penalty is closer to ~150–300 ms per long-session refresh instead of linear stacking on every page. We’ll include conservative QoS SLO language in the SOW describing expected penalties and fallbacks.

Actions:
- Marcus will attach the final workbook rows used for pricing and the latency sims (done).
- Dev will attach the SOW draft and SOC2 evidence link (working on it).
- Please confirm Plan A and we’ll return a priced SOW by EOD Wednesday.

If you want, we can do a 30-minute handoff with Orbitron infra next Tuesday to walk the exact fallback wiring and KV-offload telemetry.

—Olga
